meta.title: The G Form: Wider in Minor Than It Was in Major
meta.summary: Flattening the G form's third pushes it below the barre itself, so the widest CAGED shape gets wider still and splits into three small triads instead of one big chord.

It also got wider. A major's G form is

spans.text: So it lives in pieces, and each piece is a complete

The bottom three is a whole minor triad walking back down the frets as it climbs the strings — good under a low root. It's the piece you'd reach for if a bass note or a low E-string riff needs a full chord dropped in underneath it without a stretch.
The middle three is worth its own paragraph, because it isn't new. Look at the frets:
. That's the fretted part of the open
. The A form and the G form overlap exactly here — the same three notes, reached from two different shapes.
The top three is the most useful of the three: all three notes at fret 5, one finger laid across three strings, and a whole minor chord falls out.
Strings 3-2-1, all at fret 5, is a whole
This grip is also the only one of the five that carries the
. Every other form's grip has exactly one. It means any piece of this form that takes both of those states the chord's quality twice over rather than once.
The window itself holds eight dots, one more than A major's seven; the extra is
, which stepped in from above the window's top fret. Unlike the C form's extra dots, this one lands inside the top fragment — it's a note you actually play, not a spare.
Three roots and a chord tone on every one of the six strings mean this window shows the chord's whole range at a glance, low E to high E, without a single gap. It's a form worth

That's worth stating plainly, because it's easy to write off a shape you can never grab whole as a shape you don't need. You do need it — just not all at once. A chord you can't hold in one hand is still a chord, and three small, easy triads that happen to share a window are worth more in practice than one impossible five-fret stretch would ever be.
